User: I have a legal situation I need help thinking through. It's related to contract dispute with a former employer. I'm working with Sarah Chen from Hart & Associates; our next step is housing court. Timeline: The judge set a status conference in two months.. The other party is my former business partner. We're in Maricopa County, Arizona. I have documentation but I'm not sure what else the court will want. I'd like to know what I should ask my lawyer regarding my rights and what the next steps typically

look like. This is private legal business.
Assistant: Thanks — this is good context. Below I’ll lay out practical things to ask Sarah Chen, a checklist of documents and evidence to gather, what typically happens at a status conference in civil/housing matters in Maricopa County, and likely next steps so you can be prepared and use your meeting time efficiently. This is general informational guidance — for legal advice tailored to your situation, discuss these points with Sarah.

Key things to confirm first

with Sarah
- Which court and case type exactly (e.g., Justice Court, Superior Court, “Housing Court”/eviction division, or civil case)? Confirm venue/jurisdiction and the judge’s local rules and any required filings before the status conference.
- The legal claims and remedies you are pursuing (e.g., breach of contract, conversion, accounting, injunctive relief, damages) and any potential counterclaims the former partner might raise.
- The case timeline and deadlines the judge will likely set at the status

conference (discovery cutoff, motion deadlines, mediation/ADR, pretrial conference, trial date).
- The strategy Sarah recommends (litigate for trial, seek early settlement, pursue summary judgment, seek temporary relief).
- Your rights/defenses that are most important (statute of limitations, breach elements, defenses like waiver, accord and satisfaction, estoppel, contribution/reduction of damages).
- Evidence and discovery plan: what to request (documents, bank records, emails, communications, company rec

ords, tax returns, metadata), whether to issue subpoenas, whether depositions or expert testimony will be necessary.
- Preservation obligations: what you must keep (electronic files, devices, communications) and whether to send a legal hold notice.
- Costs and fees: likely out-of-pocket expenses (depositions, experts, filing fees), billing rate estimates, whether you can recover attorney’s fees or costs if you win.
- Settlement posture and authority: whether she recommends a demand, what settlement range is

realistic, what settlement terms you should insist on (confidentiality, release language, payment schedule).
- Practical logistics: who will attend the status conference, whether any pre-conference report or statement must be filed, and how Sarah will communicate updates to you.

Suggested specific questions to ask Sarah in your meeting
- “Which court rules and local procedures apply for our status conference and what must we file beforehand?”
- “What are the judge’s typical procedures at status conference

s in this division?”
- “What are our strongest claims and defenses? What facts or documents are the weakest points?”
- “What discovery do we need right away? Who do we need to depose and what subpoenas should we issue?”
- “Do we need an expert? If so, when should we retain one and what are the likely costs?”
- “What settlement options and ranges should I realistically expect? What are the pros/cons of settlement vs continuing?”
- “What immediate preservation steps should I take (digital and physical)? Do yo

u recommend a legal hold or notice to the other side?”
- “What motions might we anticipate (dismissal, summary judgment, motions to compel) and how do they fit into the timeline?”
- “If we win, how will judgment be enforced and what are the practical steps to collect damages?”
- “What will you need from me before the status conference (documents, signed authorizations, witness names)?”

Documents and evidence checklist to gather now
- The written contract(s), partnership agreement, bylaws, amendments, adden

da
- Any termination letters, resignation notices, or communications about ending the relationship
- All emails, text messages, instant messages, and notes related to the dispute (include dates, participants)
- Financial records: bank statements, accounting ledgers, invoices, payment records, expense reports, payroll records relevant to the dispute
- Tax returns or business filings if they show financials tied to the dispute
- Records of meetings, minutes, and contemporaneous notes
- Any prior demand letter

s, settlement offers, or offers to compromise
- Evidence of damages and mitigation: receipts, invoices, lost-profits calculations, documentation of expenses you incurred
- Witness contact info and short summary of what each can testify to
- Any previous court filings or related litigation documents
- Device preservation: export relevant metadata, preserve original files, screenshots with timestamps if needed

What to expect at the status conference (typical)
- Purpose: to update the court on case status and

to set a schedule (discovery deadlines, motion deadlines, mediation/settlement deadlines, pretrial conference, trial date).
- The judge may ask counsel whether the parties have met and confer about discovery and settlement (and may order mediation or ADR).
- The court might set a case management/scheduling order and require specific filings (e.g., initial disclosures, proposed discovery plan).
- The judge may address any immediate procedural issues (requests for extensions, motions pending) or discuss narr

owing issues to be tried.
- Often no evidence is presented at the status conference; it’s procedural. Expect scheduling and administrative directives.

Typical next steps after a status conference
- Formal scheduling order issued listing discovery cutoff, motion deadlines, mediation window, pretrial conference, and trial date.
- Exchange of disclosures and initial discoverable documents; depositions and written discovery (interrogatories, requests for production).
- Motions practice as needed (motions to co

mpel, protective orders, summary judgment).
- ADR or mediation is often ordered or recommended before trial.
- Pretrial exchanges: exhibit lists, witness lists, trial brief or pretrial statement.
- Possible settlement negotiations; if unsuccessful, trial proceeds, then post-judgment enforcement if you prevail.

Practical immediate actions for you to take
- Preserve all documents and electronic communications immediately (don’t delete anything). If unsure, keep originals and make backups.
- Create a concise

chronological timeline (one page) of key events with dates and the physical location of documents/evidence.
- Assemble the document checklist above and label exhibits.
- Note potential witnesses and brief summaries of what they will say.
- Ask Sarah if any declarations or affidavits prepared now would help—sometimes a sworn declaration from you or a witness is useful early on.
- Confirm whether any filings are due before the status conference and who will prepare them.

Questions about privacy and communica

tions
- Ask Sarah how she prefers confidential documents transmitted (secure client portal, encrypted email, in-person drop-off) and whether anything should not be sent by regular email.
- Confirm whether communications with her are protected by attorney-client privilege for all relevant facts and documents.

How I can help you right now
- I can draft a concise email or list of questions to send to Sarah summarizing these points and asking for any immediate steps she wants you to take before the conference.

- I can format your one-page chronological timeline or a documents checklist you can print and bring to the meeting.

Would you like me to draft that email to Sarah Chen for you (I can include the questions and attach the documents checklist), or prepare a one-page timeline you can review and print? If yes, tell me how formal you want the email to be and any specific items you already have that I should mention.
